To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
19F MRI can noninvasively track and quantify antigen‐specific T‐cell migration in vivo.

19F MRI can be used to non‐invasively track the trafficking of antigen‐specific T‐cell populations in a mouse model of inflammation and that this technique is applicable for the in vivo study of T‐cell migration.

(a) 19F MRI provides a means of noninvasively monitoring cell trafficking in the body; (b) PFPE nanoemulsion is a useful agent for labeling immune cells for 19F MRI; and (c) 19F MRIs are useful for monitoring the trafficking and biodistribution of immune cells.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of new MRI contrast agents for the detection of immune cells in vivo.
the development of new MRI techniques to image the immune system, specifically the T cell response.
developing and applying non-invasive imaging techniques to study the immune system, with the goal of developing new treatments for cancer.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the use of 19F MRI in combination with PFPE‐labeled cells can be used to non‐invasively track the trafficking and quantitate the numbers of a defined cell phenotype in the body.
the authors have developed a method to track and quantitatively measure the accumulation of antigen‐specific cells in a mouse lymph node.
the use of 19F MRI in vivo cytometry is a promising tool for the study of immune cell trafficking.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
19F MRI can be used to quantify the number of antigen‐specific T‐cells that have trafficked to a draining lymph node.
we were able to noninvasively track and quantify antigen-specific T cells in vivo.
we developed a method to track the movement of a specific type of T cell using MRI.
The main takeaway from our work is that
it is possible to image cells of defined phenotype in vivo using 19F magnetic resonance imaging (MRI).
it is possible to track the trafficking of a phenotypically defined cell population using a noninvasive MRI method.
we can image the biodistribution of a specific cell type in vivo.
